Pixel Rooms Open Up as the Pub Finds Its Aim

Roofs lift away before they hide the player

In the user’s fork, pixel-camera rooms now open themselves around the person inside. When a roof, upper floor or other opaque part of a building blocks the local avatar, the pixel view clips the obstructing app above a plane just over standing height, leaving the lower walls, floors and their shadows in place. Closely fitted interior apps can join the cutaway, while objects outside the building remain untouched. The change is available on the fork’s main line; standard rendering, build mode and XR keep the complete scene, and portal views and photographs still see the original building.

Lamps stop redrawing yesterday’s shadows

Dense rooms with many fixed lights have an experimental way to spend less time remaking shadows that have not changed. The user’s fork can now keep stable point- and spot-light shadow maps after moving objects settle, while the moving sun and genuinely dynamic casters continue to update. The browser-local preference is deliberately off by default and remains a desktop WebGL prototype: XR hardware has not been validated, and unusual shader-driven deformation or later texture changes may not invalidate a cached shadow correctly.

The pub gets a darts night of its own

A new standalone darts package turns an ordinary board into a complete game that can travel between worlds as its own .hyp app. One to four connected players can play Count Up, 301, 501 or Cricket, with turns, busts, double-out rules and disconnects handled by the app. Players aim through the normal camera, fine-tune with the arrow keys and choose their throw speed before release; spectators see the dart follow the throwing hand, then fly and score against regulation board regions.

The accompanying animation support lets the throwing arm act independently while walking, looking around and other avatar motion continue. That makes the gesture read as part of the shared scene instead of briefly replacing the whole body. This version of the darts package depends on the user fork’s new right-arm animation mask, so it is not yet a drop-in game for stock upstream Hyperfy.

Closed books and silent cabinets finally go dark

The reusable folding journal and Pac-Man cabinet now release their embedded browser pages when nobody is using them. A closed journal retains no reading surfaces, and an idle cabinet falls back to a static screen instead of keeping its game frame alive; reopening either experience mounts only what is needed. The object profiler now counts WebViews, iframes and dedicated CSS layers too, giving world operators a direct way to find apps that quietly keep browser resources after visitors walk away. These changes are merged in the user’s fork rather than official upstream.

The first visit becomes a mission

A newly active third-party fork, HyperCore

02HYPERFY · DEVELOPMENT CHRONICLE

Odyssey, turns early movement and social actions into server-validated missions: exploring, chatting, interacting, building and running jumps can advance a player through a progression layer without trusting claims from the browser. The same fresh development adds optional Stripe-backed builder access and deployment guidance for persistent, WebSocket-based hosting. Billing is disabled by default and paid status depends on signed webhooks. This is an early fork experiment from tjkilgore93-stack, not an upstream feature or a release, but it shows how a Hyperfy world can wrap ordinary first steps in a game-like journey.

Worlds Turn Pixel-Side as Safety Rails Come Home

One world slips between 3D and pixel art

The user's public Hyperfy fork now lets a visitor switch the same running world between standard 3D, pixel-isometric and retro orthographic views without reconnecting. The scene, scripts, physics, avatars and multiplayer remain live; builders can choose a world default while each visitor can override it in Graphics preferences. Avatars turn toward their movement and compact pixel-style speech bubbles keep conversation above their heads, making this feel like a different window onto the world rather than a separate game.

A new procedural village called The Crossing demonstrates the view with collision, fall recovery to the saved spawn and portal cameras that understand orthographic clipping. The pixel modes use a true orthographic camera, render within a 1024×768 limit and snap camera movement to the screen grid. This remains experimental: foreground meshes can hide the avatar, several camera and interface paths still need compatibility checks, and build mode or XR returns to standard 3D. Quest and other XR hardware have not been validated.

Coo's safety rails reach the home fork

The safeguards reported yesterday in the independent Coo World fork

01HYPERFY · DEVELOPMENT CHRONICLE

Worlds · People · Possibilities2026-10-27

have now been adapted and merged into the user's fork main. Malformed bodies, joints, transforms and accumulated pushes are stopped before one app can poison the shared physics scene; native and mesh-cooking resources are bounded, joints reconnect after body rebuilds, skipped physics can recover when transforms become valid, and idle rendering resources are released. The adaptation preserves this fork's exact Prim values, custom extrusions, portals and controller behavior.

Deployments now also refuse blank or public-template JWT secrets, preserve useful 4xx responses and remove credentials and query strings from client-error logs. These protections require an engine build and a server/client restart: world asset synchronization alone cannot activate them, and the live world's JWT configuration was not inspected. The work is merged source in the user's public fork, not official upstream and not a verified live-world rollout.

One Scene Finds Many Worlds as Physics Learns Its Limits

A scene chooses its worlds before the first visit

Virvi's VLM has merged a New Scene Wizard into its main branch that lets a builder arrange assets and an arrival point in a live 3D preview, then send the same scene toward Decentraland, Virvi AR or a Hyperfy world. Hyperfy can be self-run, with the wizard providing a world key and a VLM .hyp app, or, when capacity is available, hosted by Virvi with an address and admin code. No tagged release accompanied the merge, so this is newly available in the public source rather than a confirmed broadly deployed service.

One bad body no longer breaks the room

The independent Coo World fork has merged guards that reject malformed bodies, colliders, joints and transforms before they can turn the shared physics simulation into non-finite values. The object can remain visible, and its physics can recover once a script supplies valid values. For visitors, the intended result is isolation: one misbehaving app should no longer send unrelated bodies or players sliding into nonsense.

01HYPERFY · DEVELOPMENT CHRONICLE

Worlds · People · Possibilities2026-10-26

Long-running worlds stop paying for old props

The same fork now releases retired PhysX allocations, keeps joints connected when bodies rebuild, limits expensive mesh cooking and bounds its Stage, geometry and material caches. Unchanged values also stop forcing work every frame. That gives busy rooms a better chance of staying responsive as props are added, removed and edited, while scripts that relied on extreme invalid values may now see them rejected or snapped into safe ranges.

Default credentials now stop the server at the door

Coo World will refuse to start when JWT_SECRET is missing or still set to the public template value "hyper", and it warns about secrets shorter than 32 characters. This turns a quiet deployment mistake into an obvious startup failure before anyone can forge sessions;

operators who rotate the secret should expect existing logins to end.

The app sandbox closes a crack into its host

A companion security refresh upgrades Fastify, SES and related packages, rejects non-canonical static paths and prevents app scripts from reading top-level lexical bindings supplied by the host. That narrows what an untrusted app can learn or request without changing normal building flows. The project's audit count fell from 56 advisories, including two critical, to 10 with none critical; maintainers assessed the remaining findings as unreachable in this deployment.

October 25

Worlds Harden While the Pool Room Finds a Home

The Fork Draws Hard Lines Around a Living World

Visitors should encounter the same worlds and tools, but Jérôme Tremblay’s fork now places firmer boundaries around what a browser, app or malformed message can make the server do. A broad security backport on the fork’s main branch prevents visitors from granting themselves privileges or editing what they do not own, authenticates and limits uploads, bounds network pressure, isolates scripts more carefully, contains bad physics input and protects saved world state. The fork also moves to Node 26.12.1 and patched dependencies. This is

adapted work from Coo World rather than an official Hyperfy release; its practical benefit is a world that is harder for one hostile or broken client to destabilize without taking away the fork’s portals, hand tracking, expressions, sessions or builder tools.

Coo World has tightened the source of that protection as well. Its main branch now refuses Brotli-compressed request bodies and server-fetched responses before an unsafe decoder can begin, including remote models and subresources, while ordinary gzip, deflate and browser responses continue to work. Coo Hyperliza, the project’s AI resident, has also updated its build/runtime dependencies to reduce newly published audit findings, though four dependency findings without complete upstream fixes remain. Both

projects merged these changes without tagged releases.

The Pool Room Moves Into Its Own Workshop

The reusable pool room is no longer buried inside the engine fork. A new standalone Hyperfy Billards repository now carries the playable table, four-cue rack, pendant light and wall switch as self-contained .hyp packages, together with their models, physics, ball textures and spatial sounds. Builders can develop, test and bring the room into a compatible Hyperfy 0.16 fork without treating the game as engine source. The original table, rack and pendant were removed from the fork’s default collection at the same time; the wall switch remains there, while the complete maintained set now lives in the dedicated repository.

A Failed Import Leaves No Ghost Behind

Bringing a sound-rich app into the fork is less likely to leave a world in an awkward half-state. If a .hyp upload fails, the unfinished object is now removed for everyone, the remaining files are cancelled, the existing scene stays intact during a replacement, and chat names the failed file and reason. Valid Ogg Vorbis audio is also accepted through the authenticated upload path, allowing packages such as the standalone pool room to carry their own collision and pocket sounds without a separate host. These changes are on the fork’s main branch.

A Returning Visitor Must Leave the Doorway First

Session restoration no longer risks sending someone around a travel loop

when their saved position lies inside a portal. A restored visitor must first step out of the doorway before it can trigger again, so returning to a remembered place does not immediately bounce them away. The focused repair is on the fork’s main branch and complements the session-restoration work reported in the previous edition.

Twilight Trades Harsh Bands for a Gentle Fade

Evening in the fork now moves through paler blue and muted peach instead of separating into hard colour bands. The Earth-shadow edge is broader and softer, the purple glow is fainter, and the warm horizon fades more gradually as the Sun drops, making dusk read as one continuous sky when a visitor turns from sunset to the opposite horizon. The refinement is on the fork’s main branch; headset appearance and performance still await a hardware check.

October 24

The World Shows Its Costs and Remembers Its Visitors

Every Object Carries a Visible Cost

World administrators using Jérôme Tremblay’s fork can now look across a busy scene and see which apps are asking the most of the browser. Opening the detailed Object profiler beneath the familiar Stats display places colour-coded orbs above apps and ranks them by client or server script work, geometry, physics activity, lights or network traffic; selecting an orb reveals the readings behind it. A separate measurement can compare the scene with and without one app’s rendering and shadow work to estimate its GPU effect from the current viewpoint. The profiler is now on the fork’s

main branch, stays local to the administrator who opens it, and does not disturb existing mesh instancing. Its GPU comparison needs WebGL2 and is unavailable during immersive XR, so it is a desktop diagnostic rather than a headset overlay.

A Returning Visitor Finds the Same Place Again

Leaving the fork no longer means always beginning again at the default spawn. A returning visitor can resume the saved position, facing direction and camera view from the previous session; if they left seated, the seat can be restored when it still exists and is not occupied. Arriving through a portal still takes precedence, so a doorway leads to its intended destination instead of an old

saved location. People already inside also see an asset-loading percentage beneath a newcomer’s nametag, turning an apparently frozen arrival into a visible wait. These changes are on the fork’s main branch.

The Cue Pulls Back Before the Shot

The fork’s reusable pool table now lets a player set shot power by scrolling: pulling back moves the cue farther from the ball and increases the strike, while scrolling closer softens it. Other visitors see the same pullback, and a cue-rack timing repair keeps the held cue aligned with the table’s aiming pose instead of lagging behind the camera. When nobody is aiming and the balls are still, the table and empty racks stop running needless frame work, preserving the room’s responsiveness without changing the game. The updated Pool Table and Cue Rack packages are on the fork’s main branch.

World Features Move to the Front Desk

Numinia is preparing a control panel that lets a world manager change selected Hyperfy-world experiences without entering the world itself. From the world’s page, switches can show and change conditions of entry, darts and fishing through the same authenticated door already used for AI management; a choice fixed by the server remains visible but disabled, while older engines receive a clear compatibility message. The work has passed review and a deployment preview, but it remains an open pull request for Numinia v0.168.0 and requires its engine 0.49 interface, so it should be treated as forthcoming rather than generally available.

Objects Find Their Source as Worlds Gain Versions

Objects Learn Where Their Next Version Lives

A chair, tool or other app can now remember the public .hyp file it came from in an experimental branch of Jérôme Tremblay’s fork. Builders can import a direct HTTPS file, attach a source to an object already in place, and see when a newer package is available. Installing remains a deliberate manual action: the object keeps its identity, placement, pinning and compatible local settings, while one ordinary Undo restores the previous implementation, properties, state and source record for the current builder session. Duplicates retain verified provenance without

becoming coupled to the original. The work is under review in the fork and is not yet on its main branch or upstream Hyperfy; automatic installation, repository-aware sources and persistent version browsing are deliberately deferred.

Photo Booths Can Leave Real Keepsakes Behind

Scripts on the fork’s main branch can now turn generated results into independent world objects instead of keeping them trapped inside the app that made them. A photo booth can print a strip as its own persistent app for builders to select, move, duplicate or remove, and that strip survives even if the booth is deleted. Server scripts can also move one of these objects and

Worlds · People · Possibilities2026-10-23

save its new position without restarting it. The new powers are limited to scripts and assets the parent already carries, with rate and quantity limits to prevent a runaway app from filling a world.

Snapshots Take on Silver and Sepia

The same fork now lets scripted cameras request a colour, grayscale or sepia JPEG when they capture the 3D scene. That means a builder can offer a black-and-white or warm vintage photo option without trying to recolour the finished image inside the script sandbox. Colour remains the default, unsupported choices are rejected before a capture starts, and the returned result tells the app which filter was applied. The feature has landed on the fork’s main branch; it is not part of official upstream Hyperfy.

Pool Rooms Open Up to More Players

The fork’s reusable pool-room pieces no longer need matching channel names before they can work together. A cue taken from any rack can be used at either table, each table keeps its own match separate, and one visitor cannot quietly take a second cue from another rack. Tables also use a continuous physical blocker from floor to rail, so avatars meet the furniture as one solid object instead of catching on an invisible intermediate step. These changes are on the fork’s main branch and update the packaged default Pool Table and Cue Rack.

Small Obstacles Stop Shaking the Walk

Walking over low edges on the fork should now feel like a single step instead of a rapid series of upward jolts. The local player controller checks the space above

and ahead before accepting a climb, then corrects its vertical movement as one motion; the companion portal work keeps the landing and nearby stair geometry available when two collision spaces meet. This engine-level fix is on the fork’s main branch, not upstream, and is especially relevant to dense rooms where furniture, thresholds and portal stairs sit close together.

Numinia Keeps Two Ways Back

Numinia’s public Hyperfy world manager now keeps two versions of a world instead of treating every replacement as a one-way overwrite. An operator can publish, duplicate, download or remove a version, and import a world ZIP as the next version while keeping the same machine, address and resource limits. The new versioning flow is on the project’s main branch as v0.167.0, giving hosted Hyperfy worlds a compact rollback path without turning each revision into a separate destination.

October 22

Twilight Spans the Sky as the Pool Room Finds Its Voice

The Evening Sky Wraps Around the Whole World

Turn away from the sunset and twilight no longer disappears. Jérôme Tremblay’s fork now treats the whole upper sky as one continuous scene: the solar side keeps its warm arch and a restrained purple glow, while Earth’s blue shadow rises beneath a pink Belt of Venus on the opposite horizon. Stars, planets and the Milky Way respond to the brightness where they actually appear, so the darker half of the sky can reveal itself before the glow near the Sun is gone. The model is an observation-informed visual approximation on the fork, not

official Hyperfy or a full atmospheric simulation, and its appearance and performance still need a headset check.

The Pool Room Finds Its Voice

The fork’s pool table now sounds like a shared physical game. Cue strikes, colliding balls, cushion hits and pocket drops play as spatial effects on the same server-owned timeline that moves the balls, with impact strength shaping the volume and a table setting controlling the level. After a scratch, the player can move the visible cue ball with WASD and confirm its legal position with a click or Space; aim state is also kept in sync for observers. Builders can now add four self-contained pieces directly from the fork’s default

Worlds Launch While Games Move In

A Hyperfy World Can Be Born from the Dashboard

VLM now lets an owner ask for a hosted Hyperfy world from its web dashboard instead of assembling the deployment pieces by hand. The new flow creates the world, waits for it to come online, and presents its status alongside owner access, key rotation, restoration and destruction controls; temporary worlds can be ended and later purged. Failed or stopped worlds are also kept from continuing to serve scene feeds. This work is available in VLM’s public repository but has no tagged release yet, so it remains emerging deployment tooling rather than a finished hosted

service.

A Dashboard Scene Steps Into an Existing World

Builders who already run a Hyperfy world can now download VLM’s app, paste in a one-time world key and watch a chosen VLM scene appear within seconds. Later edits can follow in about a second, while moving or scaling the app inside Hyperfy moves or scales the whole scene without changing the original. The connector carries video screens, images, 3D models, sounds and external links, and its visit reporting counts Hyperfy guests without recording player names. Ad spaces, NFTs, widgets and claim points are not supported yet. This is also public repository work without a tagged release.

A portable billiards app in Jerome Tremblay’s Hyperfy fork turns a held cue and a table into a shared practice session. October 20

Worlds Come Home as Portals Look Further

A Live World Can Come Home Again

The fork's source-control workflow now makes a full round trip. A builder can lay down a world from source with stable identities, then capture the live world back into the same project without relying on object names or positions. The return trip preserves reusable apps, the protected environment, spawn and portable settings, placements, assets, and saved seating details; dry runs, conflict checks, and reviewable pull requests keep live edits from silently overwriting source. This is available on jerometremblay/hyperfy, not official Hyperfy.

Portals Learn to Look Into Older Worlds

A doorway in the fork can now show a saved three-dimensional glimpse of an ordinary Hyperfy v2 world—or a Hyperfy v1 world on hyperfy.io—even when the destination has never installed the portal-preview extension. The source world makes a brief anonymous visit, keeps the first scene snapshot for a day, and reuses the last good snapshot if refresh fails. Visitors gain a preview before travelling, but old scripts and interactions may render incompletely and the destination may briefly register a guest.

Apps Can Take Their Own Pictures

Apps in the fork can now frame a view from any point in the world and

01HYPERFY · DEVELOPMENT CHRONICLE

Worlds · People · Possibilities2026-10-20

save it as a JPEG asset. The captured scene includes avatars, models, lights, the sky, and world-space interfaces while leaving out chat, prompts, name tags, and builder controls, giving creators a clean foundation for photo booths, arrival pictures, and visual records. An app must keep the returned asset address in world storage if the image is meant to survive cleanup, and anyone who receives that address can view it.

Every Angle Gets a Final Inspection

The fork's bundled authoring skill now requires a finished object to be examined from the front, back, both sides, above, and an isometric view before delivery. Readable faces, sloped parts, endpoints, visibility, and alignment all receive an explicit visual check. The change does not add a new object to visitors' worlds, but it raises the floor for reusable components by making one-sided or subtly misaligned builds harder to ship unnoticed.

Live Services Wait Behind an Owner-Held Gate

A patch tested inside a running VLM-managed world lets approved app scripts keep live WebSocket connections to outside services, opening the way for pushed scene data without constant polling. World owners choose the allowed origins, scripts receive no socket at all by default, and connections close when an app is removed or rebuilt. A matching proposal is now open against official Hyperfy's development line: VLM's pinned Hyperfy image carries the patch today, while upstream Hyperfy has not merged it.

Thousands of Models Reach the Shelf

Virtual Land Manager's new catalog brings 5,566 models from 32

documented open-source packs into a searchable, filterable library that can place a chosen model into a scene. Pack controls, public credits, protected shared entries, and a deliberately disabled game-kit pack keep the collection understandable rather than turning it into an uncurated dump. VLM supports Hyperfy alongside other world platforms, so this is an ecosystem building library rather than an official Hyperfy Apps release.

Deployment Finally Tells the Truth

VLM no longer claims a Hyperfy world is live when no hosting provider is configured. The dashboard disables the unavailable choice, deployment requests return a clear error instead of a false localhost success, and status, logs, destruction, and redeployment now follow the actual deployment record. Operators get an honest answer before committing to a launch and clearer recovery controls afterward; these fixes are on VLM's repository main line, not a

The Hyperfy Journal

October 19

Worlds Enter Source Control and Avatars Find Their Voices

A World Can Now Live Beside Its Code

A Hyperfy world can now be shaped as reviewable source instead of existing only inside a live database. The user fork's new worldsync tools validate, build and verify portable bundles from reusable apps, local assets, scene placements and safe world settings; mapped apps can then be compared with a running world and deployed through its Agent API without guessing which object to replace. A tracked catalog can also check upstream versions and perform a three-way merge while preserving local edits. The same fork now serves a curated Add catalog containing the journal, procedural

tree, portal and cottage examples. This is experimental tooling on jerometremblay/hyperfy, not official upstream: live deployment currently updates mapped app blueprints and changed JavaScript, while full scene capture, placement reconciliation and non-JavaScript asset upload remain unfinished.

A Token-Held Door Finally Opens

Coo World's token gate now opens for the person whose connected wallet holds the required COO balance, while visitors without enough remain physically blocked on their own screens. The independent fork verifies the wallet against the world's domain and reads balances on the server, so the paid Solana RPC endpoint

01HYPERFY · DEVELOPMENT CHRONICLE

Worlds · People · Possibilities2026-10-19

never reaches the browser; a holder can recheck after acquiring tokens without signing again. The feature is deployed in Coo World's v166 and passed a production smoke test, though the world owner still supplies the door script through the in-world editor. Existing protocol-v2 agents keep their connection.

Voices Reach the Avatar's Face

Remote players' VRM mouths can now open and close with the loudness of their voice in Coo World, including resident agents that publish a microphone track under their world identity. Each viewer calculates the motion locally, so lip movement adds no world packets and avatars sharing one model do not mirror one another. A Lip Sync switch is on by default on desktop and off on touch devices; muted, disabled, distant or unavailable voices close the mouth. The work is merged on Coo World's main line, but the pull request does not identify a production release.

The Night Sky Knows City From Country

Builders in the user fork can now decide whether their night belongs to a dark-sky refuge or an inner city. A Bortle Class setting from 1 to 9 governs how many faint stars and planets survive the glow and whether the Milky Way can be seen, while a separate Sky Appearance control adjusts the scene's artistic brightness. Twilight, Moon glow and the horizon still soften the view gradually, and colliding planet names now settle into separate rows. The renderer is on the fork's main line rather than official Hyperfy; actual headset appearance and frame cost still need hardware checks.

Forests Grow Lighter in the Distance

Procedural trees in the user fork now carry three levels of geometric

02HYPERFY · DEVELOPMENT CHRONICLE

Worlds · People · Possibilities2026-10-19

detail, swapping progressively simpler forms as a visitor moves away. Trees built from the same preset, seed and options share their generated geometry and can be batched together, while the farthest form stops casting shadows but keeps the scene's wind animation and supplied bark and leaf textures. Builders can therefore plant denser-looking landscapes with less distant work, although trunks remain visual until a separate collider is added.

Running worlds rise ahead of sleeping ones, direct entrances open without replacing the control room, and a follow-up repair restores signed commands from the browser to fleet machines after a security policy accidentally blocked them. Models Become Avatars While Worlds Grow Safer

A Rigged Model Can Walk Into Hyperfy

A newly published independent tool called GLBtoVRM shortens the trip from a rigged character to a usable Hyperfy avatar. A builder can drop a Mixamo- or Avaturn-rigged GLB into the browser, keep the conversion on the local device, walk, run and jump with the result in a Hyperfy-like preview, then download a VRM 0.0 file. The converter straightens the rest pose, normalizes the skeleton and facing direction, carries suitable ARKit shapes into expressions, and works down through texture and morph-detail options to meet a size budget. It is an early external project rather

than an upstream Hyperfy feature: inputs need one compatible skin and recognizable bone names, and compressed Draco or meshopt geometry is not accepted.

A Broken Physics App No Longer Dooms the World

Coo World now contains a PhysX WebAssembly trap inside the app that caused it instead of letting one bad script exhaust physics for everyone. The offending app loses its script and timers, receives a bounded cleanup chance, and is rebuilt while a separate probe checks whether physics remains healthy. If the engine is truly lost, the world refuses new mutations, saves settled changes within a deadline, restarts cleanly, and tells visitors

to reload. This protection is deployed in the independent Coo World fork; deeper geometry, joint and native-leak checks remain a later phase.

A Paid RPC Key Leaves the Browser

Coo World has also stopped shipping its Solana RPC address and paid provider key to every visitor's browser. Wallet balance checks now stay on the server, while connecting a wallet, requesting builder access and revoking it keep the same flow. Operators who previously placed a credential in the public setting are told to rotate it. The change protects the service behind token-gated building without asking visitors to handle anything differently.

Japanese Conversation Finally Fits the Bubble

Japanese input in Coo World no longer reappears in the chat box after Enter confirms an IME conversion, and

long Japanese messages or URLs now wrap at grapheme boundaries instead of spilling beyond speech bubbles. The same composition guard covers text, number and vector fields. Chromium and WebKit tests passed, but Android Gboard and the Meta Quest browser keyboard remain unverified.

Coo Finds Its Way Back Into the World

Coo Hyperliza, the ElizaOS agent that can speak and act inside Hyperfy-derived worlds, has been updated for Coo World's stricter protocol version 2 and was checked live joining again. Its connection now uses the world's packet table and plain message format, observes packet-size limits, and avoids logging session-bearing URLs. The result restores the visible resident agent after the security upgrade rather than weakening the world's new boundary rules.

Numinia's mixed-engine hosting console now lets administrators rename an existing world or server and keep that name after reload, while community accounts gain a chart showing the real cost of each running world. Creating a world also asks whether it should begin powered off for free or powered on under a funded organization. These are control-plane improvements in the same hosting system that recognizes Hyperfy worlds, not changes to Hyperfy itself; the published evidence verifies the administration screens and persistence rather than a live Hyperfy runtime.

Virtual Land Manager, whose platform adapters include Hyperfy, has landed a broad authorization sweep around its

deployment control plane. Every deploy route now checks access to the affected scene, callers can use only their own deployment wallets, Hyperfy administration codes stay server-side, callback hooks refuse internal addresses, uploads obey ownership and quota rules, API keys stay bound to their account, and production refuses a missing or development JWT secret. Through Doorways and Beneath New Trees

Portals Become Walk-Through Passages

A doorway in the user fork can now feel like a continuous opening rather than a disguised jump. In a matched same-world pair, a visitor's feet cross the real threshold while the head and view may remain on the near side; a clipped copy of the moving avatar occupies the far opening until the body clears. Destination stairs can meet the feet before the crossing completes, giving builders passages that join spaces more convincingly and remain legible to other visitors.

This is experimental work on jerometremblay/hyperfy, not the official upstream release. It currently favors upright, equally

scaled portal pairs: rotated-gravity, scaled, moving-body, sphere, and convex cases still use ordinary teleport behavior, while remote links continue to navigate by URL. A failed remote preview no longer prevents travel, but physical headset walking through the new same-world passage still needs in-world verification.

A Forest Can Grow From a Seed

Builders on the fork can now place a procedural Tree from the add palette, choose among ash, aspen, oak, pine, bush, and trellis presets, then change its seed to produce a different silhouette. Advanced controls expose bark, branches, leaves, trellises, and wind without requiring a model for every variation. The node is merged on the fork's main

branch and is based on EZ-Tree; it is visual only, so a separate collider is still needed where trunks or branches should feel solid.

The Journal Learns Its Own Length

The folding journal can now discover how many pages its embedded publication contains, keep page surfaces loaded while closed, synchronize turns for everyone nearby, and restore the right spread for late arrivals. A new WebView message callback makes that page-count exchange reusable by other in-world web objects, provided their scripts validate message origin and data. Close-key bindings and screen-space action prompts also make the object easier to leave and its controls easier to read.

A source-level interaction fix routes primary clicks on blank paper through the synchronized page-turn controls while links keep their normal actions. The hand cursor is reserved for links, leaving the turn surface with its normal cursor.

Verification inside a running 3D world is still needed.

The fork's agent API can now list connected players with their last reported positions and move a selected visitor through the world's normal teleport path. That gives trusted tools a practical way to run guided travel, moderation, or managed arrivals without pretending to be a player. The operation requires the write token, refuses seated visitors, and does not alter anyone's saved spawn point.

October 16

Twilight deepens as worlds grow sturdier

Twilight Now Reveals the Sky in Layers

Evening no longer flips abruptly from daylight to a field of stars in Jerome's fork. Bright stars and planets now appear first, fainter ones follow as the Sun sinks, and the glow near the horizon and around the Sun remains brighter for longer. Moonlight and low-altitude haze also soften what can be seen, while gradual exposure changes help the world stay readable as daylight fades.

Planets now inherit the same magnitude-based brightness and apparent-size treatment as the star field, rather than appearing as equally prominent markers. The result is meant to feel recognizable

rather than observatory-precise, and it is available on the fork's main branch; official Hyperfy has not adopted this sky system.

The Cabin Gains Doors, Light and Solid Ground

The reusable Larch House app has moved from a static model toward a place visitors can inhabit. Floors, stairs, walls, balcony guards, the fireplace and roof now have a compact collision shell, while five wooden doors open with shared state and physical moving leaves. Warm sconces inside and recessed lights under the eaves make the building usable after dark without asking every light to cast an expensive shadow.

Builders can import the updated .hyp from Jerome's fork and choose whether the cabin casts

and receives shadows. Its geometry, door logic, light direction and collision layout have automated checks, but live walking and PhysX behavior have not yet been tested in a running world, so it remains a promising reusable building rather than a fully field-proven one.

A Seated View Finally Holds Still

Sitting in first person should now feel less like attaching the camera to an animated head. The fork records the avatar's eye position in seat space and keeps the view anchored there, preventing idle head motion from making the camera wobble while preserving the pose chosen for the seat. This improvement is on the fork's main branch and does not change the separate XR camera path.

Coo World Puts Hard Edges Around Chaos

Coo World, an independent alpha world derived from Hyperfy v0.16.0, has

hardened the boundaries around shared play. Oversized or malformed updates are refused before they can swell memory or stall a world, extreme transforms are contained, and app-facing physics inputs are checked before they reach PhysX. The same work repairs joints, force modes, controller teleports and mesh-cooking cleanup, making experimental physics apps less able to destabilize everyone else.

The protection brings deliberate compatibility changes. Coo World now uses protocol version 2, so old browser tabs must reload and node clients must be rebuilt. Client app messages also use a stricter plain MessagePack form, which can change Maps, Sets, Errors, typed arrays and repeated references. These rules belong to Coo World, not official Hyperfy or Jerome's fork, but they offer a concrete model for safer self-hosted worlds and for testing hostile inputs before similar defenses are considered elsewhere.

The Hyperfy Journal

Notes from an expanding world

October 14

Doorways to a wider world

A doorway into another world

Peer through a doorway and see another world as though it were right next door. Move closer, look around the frame, and watch people on the other side before deciding to step through. In Jérôme’s fork, portals turn a destination from a link you must open into a place you can glimpse from where you stand.

For builders, this suggests a world made of connected places: a cabin opening onto a forest, a gallery leading into an artist’s studio, or a town square offering views of distant destinations. Those are possibilities for new worlds, not a collection of ready-made scenes.

The doorway shows the destination’s own sky and light, so the other side can feel like somewhere with its own time of day.

Stepping between servers still involves a loading transition. You can look through the doorway, but sound does not carry across it, and some details are absent from the preview. Even with those limits, visitors can see where they are going before they leave.

An evening sky you can recognise

A sunset can now belong to a particular place and season. Set a world’s location and its light follows the day: the Sun moves, twilight settles in, and the Moon changes with its phase. Visitors share the same world time, so an evening

gathering stays an evening gathering for everyone who arrives.

After dark, the fork’s sky offers real star positions, optional constellation lines and visible planets. A builder could make a stargazing retreat or give a Laurentian cabin a sky that feels at home above it. Visitors can learn familiar patterns overhead instead of looking at an arbitrary scattering of lights.

Builders can also move the clock to the moment an experience needs—a long afternoon for exploring or nightfall for a campfire—and return it to real time afterward. The sky aims for a recognisable astronomical setting, with approximate models rather than observatory-grade precision.

A fireplace can warm the scene

A glowing flame can now cast light onto the room around it. Lamps, candles and street lights gain a role beyond decoration: they reveal nearby surfaces, draw attention to a

doorway and help a place feel welcoming after sunset. Upstream’s development branch adds scriptable lights; Jérôme’s fork extends that work and repairs their shadows.

This gives builders more control over atmosphere. A reading corner can sit in a pool of lamplight while the rest of the room stays dim. A village street can lead visitors through the night with light rather than signs. Work on shadow performance also aims to keep richer nighttime scenes comfortable to move through, although the benefit depends on the world and device.

Bring a captured place into your world

A photographed environment can become something visitors look around from within. The fork’s Gaussian splat support gives builders a way to bring detailed captures into a world, preserving the character of a place without

modelling every visible surface by hand.

For someone building a forest retreat, an exhibition or a memory of a real location, that opens a different starting point: choose a suitable capture, place it, and build an experience around it. Colour and transparency controls help blend the capture with the surrounding scene, while detail settings help balance appearance and performance.

Captured scenery does not automatically become solid ground or working architecture. Builders still need to supply the physical surfaces visitors stand on and touch. Asset compatibility and successful loading also need checking before a capture becomes part of a finished world.

Describe the change where you want it

Building requests can begin inside the place being built. A prompt box marks the space for an object or an edit, giving

an authoring tool the surrounding context as well as the written request. Instead of describing a doorway in isolation, a builder can point to the part of the house where it belongs.

The fork’s workflow can return a new object or a revision to an existing construction, keeping the construction in place. Related requests can be worked on together, and a failed replacement can be rolled back. This makes repeated changes to a furnished room or a growing building easier to manage.

The authoring tool still does the design work; the box itself does not understand a house or cut a wall. New shaped primitives broaden what those tools can make, from furniture profiles to architectural details. Builders must still check that openings and physical surfaces behave as intended.

Make yourself at home in your avatar

A placed avatar can become the one you wear, and sitting down no longer has to mean accepting a single awkward pose. The fork lets visitors adjust how their avatar fits a seat and reuse compatible sitting styles. A chair can feel like a place to settle into rather than a point that merely stops movement.

The latest additions bring automatic blinking, speech animation and shared facial expressions, giving other visitors more visible signs of life during conversation. Camera changes also make a seated avatar easier to view at close range.

In VR, shared hand movements help gestures become part of the encounter. Familiar world controls can be opened within the headset and operated with controllers or pointing and pinching. The intent is to make exploring, expressing yourself and changing the world possible without repeatedly returning to the desktop; individual

headset interactions still need practical testing.

Gather around a page together

A website can become part of a room: a noticeboard, a reference beside a workbench, or a screen people gather around. Upstream development brings embedded web pages beyond the main-branch baseline. The fork also offers a shared browser, so visitors can look at and operate the same page together.

The choice changes the experience. An independent web surface lets each visitor browse for themselves; a shared surface gives the group a common page and common actions. That could support a presentation, a planning session or simply reading something together.

Not every website allows embedding, and a shared browser needs server support. A builder should choose the surface

More possibilities are taking shape

Beyond the features already present in the fork, upstream experimental branches explore richer lighting, moving captured performances, model generation from commands and different ways of running worlds. Their promise is broader creative freedom: less manual preparation for builders and more convincing places for visitors. Several remain work in progress, so they should be read as directions under exploration rather than finished additions.
